section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Vectors as Arrows
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed arrows in 2D space (R²). Visualize vector addition as the 'tip-to-tail' method and scalar multiplication as scaling the length.
section_1.example: Representing a character's movement: Vector A (2 units right) + Vector B (1 unit up) = Resultant jump.

section_2.title: Linear Combinations and Span
section_2.content: Define a linear combination as scaling and adding vectors. Introduce 'Span' as the set of all possible points reachable by combining given vectors (a line, a plane, or the whole space).
section_2.example: A robot arm with two joints: The 'Span' represents the entire reachable area (a 2D disk) the claw can touch.

section_3.title: The Concept of Linear Dependence
section_3.content: Explain linear dependence visually: two vectors are dependent if they lie on the same line (collinear). If a new vector adds no new 'reach' to the span, it is redundant.
section_3.example: If two supply drones fly in the exact same direction, one is redundant; they don't expand the 'reach' of your delivery network.

section_4.title: Defining a Basis
section_4.content: Introduce Basis as the 'minimalist' set: vectors that are linearly independent (no redundancy) and span the entire space. It is the most efficient coordinate system.
section_4.example: Using standard basis vectors i=(1,0) and j=(0,1) as a grid map to pinpoint the exact location of a treasure chest.

section_5.title: Summary & Visual Connection
section_5.content: Synthesize the concepts: Span (the reachable area), Independence (no waste), and Basis (the building blocks). Visual animation showing the collapse of a 3D space to a 2D plane if a basis vector is lost.
section_5.example: A 3D crane loses a pivot; if the vectors become linearly dependent, the crane loses a dimension of movement.
